summary: Describes how to register a domain with the Network Information Center of the DDN and gives guidelines for setting up and running a domain, following the requirements of RFC 920. It recommends these guidelines for administrators of second-level domains, whose role is coordinator, manager and technician.

eli5.summary: If a domain is a neighborhood, this memo is the instruction sheet for the person in charge of it: how to sign up and how to keep it running.

subtitle: A practical guide to registering a domain with the NIC and running it as a domain administrator.

tldr.problem: Organizations joining the DDN and DARPA domain naming system needed to know how to register a domain and what running one involves.
tldr.mechanism: The memo describes the domain administrator and technical contact roles, the NIC's policies, the top-level domains and how to apply by electronic mail using a ten-item questionnaire.
tldr.outcome: It gives guidelines in line with RFC 920 for administrators of second-level domains, including a recommended name length of 12 characters or fewer and at least two independent servers.

today: The unit metadata lists the status of RFC 1032 as Unknown, with no recorded obsoleting or updating RFC. It is a 1987 guide written for the DDN and DARPA portions of the Internet and should be read alongside RFC 920 and RFC 1034.

sections.title: The Domain Administrator and Zone Contact
sections.content:
Domains are administrative entities giving decentralized management of host naming and addressing. The NIC was designated by the Defense Communications Agency to provide registry services for the DDN and DARPA parts of the Internet, to run the root name servers, and to administer the top-level domains ARPA, COM, EDU, ORG, GOV and MIL until other organizations could take over.

The domain administrator (DA) is coordinator, manager and technician. The DA registers with the management of the domain directly above, must be technically competent to run a domain server as described in RFC 1034, keeps the data current, handles complaints about the name server and acts on reports of misbehaving hosts. The DA also controls name assignments, checking that names are unique and follow naming conventions.

The technical and zone contact looks after the name server, resolver software and database files. A zone is the contiguous part of the domain tree for which a server has complete information and authority.
sections.eli5: The administrator is the neighborhood manager: signs people up, keeps the list right and answers complaints. The technical contact keeps the machines running.

sections.title: NIC Policies and Naming Rules
sections.content:
Domain and host name choices are local matters. The NIC will not referee disputes over who has the right to register a name, and expects local conflicts to be settled before registration. It will answer technical questions but not arbitrate.

Host names should follow RFC 952. Each segment of a domain name may contain up to 64 characters, but the NIC strongly advises 12 characters or fewer, because longer names make mistakes more likely and are harder to remember and type. Assignments are first-come-first-served. The NIC does not register individual hosts directly under the top-level domains it administers, so that administration can be delegated down the tree and subdomains keep responsibility for their hosts.

Countries wanting a top-level domain must use the two-letter code from ISO-3166. Where that clashes with a U.S. Postal Service state code, requests for the three-letter form will be considered.
sections.eli5: The registry will not settle fights about who gets a name. Pick a short name, because short ones are easier to remember and type.

sections.title: Choosing a Top-Level Domain
sections.content:
The top-level domains registered with the DDN NIC were ARPA, COM, EDU, GOV, MIL, NET and ORG, plus a number of country domains. Each has an intended purpose.

  • ARPA: a temporary domain appended by default to hosts not yet in a domain. In 1984 the label was added to every host name in the Official DoD Internet Host Table to speed the transition.
  • COM: companies and businesses.
  • EDU: universities and other educational institutions.
  • GOV: government agencies.
  • MIL: military organizations.
  • NET: network service centers, consortia, information centers and operations centers.
  • ORG: organizations that do not clearly fit elsewhere, such as technical-support groups or professional societies.

A host should have only one name regardless of the networks it is on, so domain names should not include routing information or addresses. Domain name syntax is in Section 3 of RFC 1034.
sections.eli5: Each top-level name is like a section of a library: companies here, schools there, government somewhere else. Pick the shelf that fits you.

sections.title: How to Register and Verify
sections.content:
To register, obtain the domain questionnaire from the NIC hostmaster or FTP NETINFO:DOMAIN-TEMPLATE.TXT from SRI-NIC.ARPA, fill it out completely and return it by electronic mail to HOSTMASTER@SRI-NIC.ARPA. The application should come from the person administratively responsible for the domain. Hostmaster personnel review it, and the RFC expects a few rounds of email before the domain is authorized. The DA must keep the data current with the NIC or with a registration agent. CSNET and UUCP, for example, act as domain filters for their own organizations.

The questionnaire asks for the top-level domain to join, administrative and technical contacts (by NIC handle), the domain name (up to 12 characters), a description of the servers and their start date, host names and addresses of the servers, planned mapping of other hosts into the new name space, estimated host counts now and over one, two and five years, the date the fully qualified name should become official in HOSTS.TXT, and a description of the organization. Domains must provide at least two independent servers, preferably in physically separate locations and on different PSNs.

Registered data can be checked with the NIC WHOIS server using whois domain <domain name>, or by electronic mail to SERVICE@SRI-NIC.ARPA. Further information is in online files such as NETINFO:DOMAINS.TXT, or by querying the NIC Host Name Server on port 101 with the command ALL-DOM.
sections.eli5: You fill out a form, email it to the registry and answer a few follow-up questions. You must also promise to run at least two servers, so the neighborhood still works if one breaks.
